```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(cli.num_colors = 1)
```

`contactdataformat` checks whether a social contact survey dataset follows the
SOCRATES data-formatting guidelines, the layout that `socialmixr` and the
SOCRATES tools read. It validates format and internal consistency, not
scientific quality, and it never modifies the data.

```{r setup}
library(contactdataformat)
```

`write_survey()` writes the dictionary as a `.csv` file, but the dictionary of
a published record must be a spreadsheet (`.xlsx`, one sheet per file). This
helper writes a synthetic survey and converts the dictionary, so the examples
below look like a real record.

```{r helper}
write_record <- function(tables, dir, nametag) {
  write_survey(tables, dir, nametag = nametag)
  csv <- file.path(dir, paste0(nametag, "_dictionary.csv"))
  if (!requireNamespace("openxlsx", quietly = TRUE) || !file.exists(csv)) {
    return(invisible(dir))
  }
  wb <- openxlsx::createWorkbook()
  for (id in unique(tables$dictionary$file)) {
    sheet <- tables$dictionary[tables$dictionary$file == id,
                               c("variable", "description", "type", "values")]
    names(sheet) <- c("Variable", "Description", "Data type", "Allowed values")
    openxlsx::addWorksheet(wb, id)
    openxlsx::writeData(wb, id, sheet)
  }
  openxlsx::saveWorkbook(wb, file.path(dir, paste0(nametag, "_dictionary.xlsx")))
  file.remove(csv)
  invisible(dir)
}
```

## A valid dataset

`example_survey()` builds a small, fully synthetic dataset. `write_survey()`
writes it in the guideline file layout.

```{r valid}
dir <- withr::local_tempdir()
write_record(example_survey(), dir, "DOE_2012_BELGIUM")
list.files(dir)

report <- check_contact_data(dir, quiet = TRUE)
report
```

The status is `PASS`. The manual checklist lists items that software cannot
judge (for example whether the NAMETAG is the right one); they never change the
status.

## A faulty dataset

Here the contact ID is called `contact_id` (the guideline draft used three
different names; the canonical name is `cnt_id`, and the legacy spelling
`cont_id` is accepted as long as a record uses one spelling in all its files), one contact has all locations `FALSE`, and a ZIP code ended
up in the participant extra file.

```{r faulty}
tables <- example_survey()
names(tables$contact)[names(tables$contact) == "cnt_id"] <- "contact_id"
tables$contact[1, c("cnt_home", "cnt_work", "cnt_school", "cnt_transport",
                    "cnt_leisure", "cnt_otherplace")] <- FALSE
tables$participant_extra$zip_code <- "1000"

bad <- withr::local_tempdir()
write_record(tables, bad, "DOE_2012_BELGIUM")
check_contact_data(bad, quiet = TRUE)
```

Use `as.data.frame(report)` for the findings, `summary(report)` for counts, and
`report_write()` to write Markdown, CSV or JSON, for example to attach to a
Zenodo submission.

```{r write}
out <- report_write(check_contact_data(bad, quiet = TRUE),
                    file.path(bad, "check.md"))
head(readLines(out), 3)
```

## Several datasets at once: `run_check()`

`run_check()` is the one-call entry point for RStudio and scripts. Point it at
a folder with one sub-folder per dataset (one NAMETAG per sub-folder), or at a
single dataset folder. It checks every dataset, writes a report per dataset
and a table `check_summary.csv`, and prints the summary. The data are only
read: the reports go to a separate folder (`check_reports` next to or inside
the folder you give), never into a dataset folder.

```{r run-check}
root <- withr::local_tempdir()
dir.create(file.path(root, "DOE_2012_BELGIUM"))
dir.create(file.path(root, "ROE_2013_FRANCE"))
write_record(example_survey(), file.path(root, "DOE_2012_BELGIUM"),
             "DOE_2012_BELGIUM")
write_record(tables, file.path(root, "ROE_2013_FRANCE"), "ROE_2013_FRANCE")

run <- run_check(root)
list.files(run$output_dir)
```

The result is a `socrates_run` object (returned invisibly): `run$summary` has
one row per dataset, `run$reports` holds the full reports, named by dataset.

```{r run-check-details}
run$summary
as.data.frame(run$reports[["ROE_2013_FRANCE"]])[, c("rule_id", "severity", "column")]
```

Useful arguments: `output_dir` (where the reports go), `formats` (any of
`"csv"`, `"md"`, `"json"`), `write = FALSE` (only print and return),
`show = "errors"` or `"all"` (print the findings per dataset, not only the
summary), `smoke_test = TRUE`, and the arguments of `check_contact_data()`
such as `skip` and `waive`. An example script for RStudio, which installs the
package when needed, is installed with the package:

```{r example-script, eval = FALSE}
file.edit(system.file("examples", "run_check_example.R",
                      package = "contactdataformat"))
```

## Booleans: TRUE/FALSE only

Yes/no variables (locations, `phys_contact`, `holiday`, ...) are written as
`TRUE` or `FALSE`, and nothing else. The legacy `0`/`1` coding of older records
(POLYMOD, CoMix, Zenodo v1.2) and text codes such as `Y`/`N` or `yes`/`no` are
errors (rule R08), because filters would silently match nothing.

```{r boolean}
legacy <- example_survey()
legacy$contact$phys_contact <- as.integer(legacy$contact$phys_contact)
legacy$contact$cnt_home <- ifelse(legacy$contact$cnt_home, "yes", "no")
as.data.frame(check_tables(legacy$participant, legacy$contact, legacy$hh,
                           legacy$sday, quiet = TRUE))[, c("rule_id", "severity", "column")]
```

## Rules, severities and waivers

`list_rules()` is the rule catalogue. Classes: `A` automatic (schema driven),
`X` cross-table, `H` heuristic (reported as warnings), `M` manual.

```{r rules}
head(list_rules(), 8)
```

A rule that does not apply to your survey can be waived, with a reason. The
finding stays in the report as `waived`.

```{r waive}
check_contact_data(bad, quiet = TRUE,
                   waive = c(R13 = "kindergarten-only contacts, see dictionary"))$counts
```

## The schema is the specification

File names, columns, types, allowed values, keys, severities and thresholds
live in a versioned YAML file bundled with the package
(`inst/schema/socrates-guidelines-1.0.yaml`). Choices that are still open in
the guideline are listed by `open_decisions()` together with the schema key
that encodes the current choice. To try another choice, copy the file, edit it
and pass the path:

```{r decisions}
open_decisions()
```

```{r custom, eval = FALSE}
check_contact_data(dir, schema = "my-schema.yaml")
```

The package version follows the guideline version: `1.0.z` implements guideline
`1.0`.

## Keeping restricted geography out of the public record

`socialmixr` merges every CSV in a dataset that shares a column name (for
example `part_id`) with the participant or contact table. A restricted file
with ZIP codes or coordinates in the same folder would therefore be loaded, and
published, with the survey. Rule R27 flags geography column names (ZIP, address,
coordinates), restricted-looking files and values that look like postal codes
or coordinates. Finer geography belongs in a separate restricted file that is
never part of the public folder.

## Smoke test with socialmixr

With `smoke_test = TRUE`, rule R22 loads the files with
`socialmixr::load_survey()` and computes a small contact matrix.

```{r smoke, eval = requireNamespace("socialmixr", quietly = TRUE)}
check_contact_data(dir, smoke_test = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)$status
```

## Checking real data locally

Real survey data are never part of this repository. To check a local export,
point to the folder, for example through an environment variable:

```{r flanders, eval = FALSE}
check_contact_data(Sys.getenv("CONTACTDATAFORMAT_FLANDERS_DIR"))

# or all datasets in a folder, with reports written next to it
run_check("path/to/folder_with_datasets")
```
